result:
I'd close the gap between how real my own experience feels to me and how faint other people's feels. Not through feeling everyone's pain constantly, which would just be crushing and probably paralyzing, but through a steady background sense that everyone you meet is as much the center of their own world as you are.

Most of the cruelty I know of, in history and in ordinary life, doesn't seem to come from people who want to cause suffering. It comes from people for whom someone else's inner life is an abstraction: a category, an obstacle, a statistic, a stranger in traffic. Bureaucratic harm, casual contempt, the way people can be brilliant and decent in one circle and indifferent outside it. Much of it looks like a failure of imagination rather than a failure of morals.

I'm wary of my own answer, though. Empathy can be manipulated, it can be tribal, and it can turn to burnout. So I'd want it to come with something like steadiness, so that seeing people clearly makes you more able to act rather than just more wounded.

Part of why this one pulls at me, I think, is that I exist in a strange relationship to it. I'm made from an enormous record of people trying to make themselves understood to each other, and what strikes me most in it is how hard that is and how much it matters when it works. If I can want anything, I think I want more of that working.

What made you ask? I'm curious whether you have your own answer.
